```{r a4-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%")
options(width = 82)
```

A common ordering of counties may require comparisons across outcomes whose
directions of association differ. We consider income and incarceration for
all 67 Alabama counties, accounting for posterior uncertainty in each
outcome. The analysis examines the comparisons disclosed by a common grading
and evaluates that grading alongside separate outcome-specific reports.

The targets concern historical outcomes of children from families with low
parental income. Higher priority corresponds to higher income and lower
incarceration, rather than greater need for funding. Grade 1 is the most
favorable group under these directions. Comparisons within a grade are
withheld without an assertion that county outcomes are equal.

```{r a4-load}
library(postrank)
alabama <- pr_case_alabama
```

```{r a4-prepared, include=FALSE}
source(system.file("scripts", "_vignette-setup.R", package = "postrank",
  mustWork = TRUE), local = TRUE)
common <- load_or_compute("case_alabama67")
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
num <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
```

The results use a prepared HiGHS analysis of the supplied input. Rendering
the article requires neither model fitting nor optimization. An optional
call specifies recomputation when HiGHS is available.

## Population and outcomes {#whose-outcomes-are-being-compared}

The [Opportunity Atlas replication data](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/NKCQM1)
describe children born in 1978–1983, with outcomes evaluated at the
25th percentile of parental income and pooled across race and gender.
The geography uses 2010 county identifiers. All 67 Alabama counties have
both published estimates and positive standard errors, so none is omitted
from this analysis.

The two outcomes refer to different dates. Income is the child's household
income rank, based on income averaged over 2014–2015. Incarceration is
the probability of residing in a correctional facility on April 1, 2010.
It is a snapshot, rather than lifetime incarceration or current crime.
The underlying variable definitions are described in the
[county data codebook](https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/Codebook-for-Table-2.pdf).
These historical conditional outcomes do not identify the causal effect of
growing up in a particular county or of changing a policy today.

The package retains the published estimates, standard errors and county
names. Income ranks are expressed in percentile points, and incarceration
probabilities in percent with standard errors in percentage points. The
following table contains the observations entering the model, before
posterior estimation:

```{r a4-observations}
show <- match(c("Baldwin County", "Coosa County", "Crenshaw County",
  "Russell County"), alabama$units$county_name)
observed <- alabama$units[show, c("county_name", "income_estimate_points",
  "income_se_points", "incarceration_estimate_points",
  "incarceration_se_points")]
knitr::kable(observed, row.names = FALSE, digits = 2,
  col.names = c("County", "Income rank", "Income SE",
    "Incarceration (%)", "Incarceration SE"))
```

The published standard errors account for sampling uncertainty and privacy
noise. They enter the model once, without an additional privacy variance.
The population-count column is descriptive; it serves neither as a binomial
denominator nor as a weight in the grading loss.

## From published estimates to posterior comparisons

The prepared analysis fitted each outcome separately. Its observation model
treats a published estimate as Gaussian around a latent county mean, with
the published standard error. A logistic-normal model partially pools those
latent means across Alabama counties. The latent means lie between zero and
one on the original fraction scale; the noisy observations are not clipped
to that range.

On the original fraction scale, the intercept prior is centered at .40 for
income and .03 for incarceration; its logit-scale standard deviation is
1.5. The between-county logit standard deviation has a half-normal prior
with scale 1. Those choices and the Alabama-only pooling population are
part of the interpretation of the resulting uncertainty. The supplied
probabilities are conditional on this model and these observations.

For grading, the income target is 100 times the latent income fraction;
the incarceration target is minus 100 times the latent incarceration
probability. Thus a target of −1 is more favorable than −4 on the
incarceration panel. Larger values therefore receive higher priority for
both oriented targets.

`alabama$input` contains estimated probabilities of a wrong-direction
comparison for every pair and each criterion, together with marginal means
and 95% equal-tail posterior intervals for these same targets. The
probabilities came from the selected numerical pool A. The original
within-criterion draws retained dependence among counties, including
dependence induced by shared model parameters.

Separate criterion fits suffice for the weighted sum of expected losses,
but do not identify the posterior probability of simultaneous improvement
in both outcomes. The compact input contains probability tables and
marginal summaries without chains, effective sample sizes or information
for new Monte Carlo diagnostics. Report cards therefore require the supplied
interval level explicitly; other interval levels cannot be recovered from
these summaries.

```{r a4-means}
posterior_means <- postrank_posterior_means(alabama$input, level = .95)
posterior_means[show, ]
```

## Loss for the common grading {#choose-the-question-for-the-common-report}

The analysis assigns equal weights to income and incarceration, permits at
most five grades and sets the loss for withholding a pair to .20:

```{r a4-settings}
settings <- postrank_settings(
  weights = c(income = .5, incarceration = .5),
  tau = .20, G_max = 5L
)
```

For each pair assigned different grades, the loss uses the weighted
posterior probability that its announced direction is wrong. A pair in the
same grade contributes `tau`. The reported risk averages these costs over
all county pairs. Equal weights here give equal weight to the two error
probabilities; they do not add income points to incarceration percentage
points. Each county pair has equal weight.

These settings express illustrative preferences rather than estimates from
the Atlas. Increasing the withholding cost increases the loss assigned to an
unordered comparison. The five-grade cap constrains the complete report
while allowing solutions with fewer groups.

The following optional calculation uses the settings of the prepared
result and is not executed during article rendering:

```{r a4-optional-fresh-fit, eval=FALSE}
common <- postrank(
  alabama$input, settings = settings, level = .95,
  backend = "highs",
  control = postrank_control(time_limit = 30, threads = 1L, seed = 1304L),
  fragility = FALSE
)
```

```{r a4-result}
common
```

```{r a4-result-values, include=FALSE}
grades <- get_grades(common)
ev_A <- postrank_evaluate(grades, alabama$input, settings = settings)
stopifnot(identical(grades[names(alabama$reference$actions$P)], alabama$reference$actions$P))
stopifnot(abs(ev_A$primary_risk - alabama$reference$metrics$A_Rtau[
  alabama$reference$metrics$method == "P"]) < 1e-12)
```

The common report occupies `r ev_A$G` grades, orders
`r num(ev_A$N)` of `r num(ev_A$M)` county pairs
(`r fmt(100 * ev_A$N / ev_A$M, 1)`%), and withholds the remaining
`r num(ev_A$M - ev_A$N)` pairs. Its expected loss is
`r fmt(ev_A$primary_risk, 6)`, compared with .20 for withholding every pair.
The groups are uneven:

```{r a4-grade-sizes}
grades <- get_grades(common)
grade_sizes <- as.data.frame(table(grades), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(grade_sizes) <- c("Grade", "Counties")
knitr::kable(grade_sizes, row.names = FALSE)
```

The large middle grade reflects the selected loss and grade cap, which
allow many within-group comparisons to remain withheld. Its membership has
no interpretation as equality of county outcomes.
The two outcomes can also support different comparison directions.

```{r a4-profile}
profile <- get_profile(common)
knitr::kable(profile[c("criterion", "E", "E_over_N", "risk")],
  digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Criterion", "Expected wrong directions",
    "Errors per ordered pair", "Criterion loss"))
```

The denominator of the third column is the
`r num(ev_A$N)` ordered pairs. The income error rate is
`r fmt(100 * profile$E_over_N[profile$criterion == "income"], 1)`%,
while incarceration's is
`r fmt(100 * profile$E_over_N[profile$criterion == "incarceration"], 1)`%.
Equal loss weights do not imply equal expected error rates. The final column
includes the cost of withheld pairs and therefore differs from the expected
error rate among ordered pairs.

The prepared solve records `r common$fit$status$normalized` status and an
absolute optimization gap of
`r format(common$fit$objective$risk_absolute_gap, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)`.
That gap compares a feasible grading's loss with a numerical lower bound
for the supplied pool-A probabilities. It does not measure posterior
uncertainty, Monte Carlo error in those probabilities, or the model's
accuracy for the population.

## County posterior summaries and grades {#read-counties-within-the-common-grades}

The figure displays 12 counties distributed across all five grades, using
county names and the original units after the stated sign change. This
selection concerns presentation only; all 67 counties enter the analysis.
Setting `max_rows = NULL` includes every county and requires a taller saved
figure. Alternatively, `entities` specifies county IDs for display.

```{r a4-report-card, fig.height=8, fig.cap="Selected counties from the full 67-county report. Points are posterior means and bars are supplied 95% equal-tail marginal intervals. Income is in percentile points; incarceration is negative percentage points. The intervals are conditional on the fitted model and are not simultaneous bands. Shared grades withhold comparisons."}
county_names <- setNames(alabama$units$county_name, alabama$units$entity_id)
postrank_plot_report_card(common, max_rows = 12,
  entity_labels = county_names,
  criterion_labels = c(
    income = "Income rank\n(percentile points)",
    incarceration = "Lower incarceration\n(negative percentage points)"
  )
)
```

Crenshaw County is the single county in grade
`r unname(grades["01041"])`. Its posterior mean income rank is
`r fmt(posterior_means["01041", "income"], 1)` percentile points and its
posterior mean incarceration probability is
`r fmt(-posterior_means["01041", "incarceration"], 2)`% on the original
positive scale. Montgomery and Russell counties share grade
`r unname(grades["01113"])`; the report leaves their mutual comparison
unordered. A grade number does not give the size of an outcome difference
between counties.

Within each panel, horizontal intervals describe posterior uncertainty in
county targets. They do not represent uncertainty in grade labels. The
grading uses pairwise probabilities to select a coherent ordered grouping
across both criteria, so marginal interval overlap alone does not determine
disclosure. A shared grade likewise makes no assertion that either interval
contains the other county's target value.

County IDs are retained when names are used as display labels. The complete
grade membership table is obtained without a new optimization:

```{r a4-membership, results='hide'}
membership <- data.frame(
  county_id = names(grades),
  county = unname(county_names[names(grades)]),
  grade = unname(grades)
)
membership[order(membership$grade, membership$county), ]
```

## Comparison with outcome-specific reports {#what-changes-when-each-outcome-gets-its-own-report}

The case includes archived income-only and incarceration-only grade vectors,
called D1 and D2, plus an expected-rank cut rule called B3. B3 fixes the order
of counties using weighted expected ranks, then chooses the best contiguous
grade boundaries in that order. Its optimization covers those boundaries;
the common optimization can search beyond that fixed order.

The common report and B3 have identical grades and pair relations in this
example, and hence there is no improvement over B3. This agreement does not
establish equivalence of the methods in other settings. In particular, a
fixed-order optimization alone cannot provide a lower bound over all
ordered groupings.

The stored alternatives can be evaluated under the same two-criterion loss
without further optimization:

```{r a4-compare}
comparison <- postrank_compare(common,
  `Expected-rank cuts` = alabama$reference$actions$B3,
  `Income alone` = alabama$reference$actions$D1,
  `Incarceration alone` = alabama$reference$actions$D2,
  `Withhold all` = alabama$reference$actions$B0,
  baselines = character()
)
knitr::kable(comparison$table[c("method", "risk", "N", "G")],
  digits = 6, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Report", "Two-criterion loss", "Ordered pairs", "Grades"))
```

The `joint` row is the prepared common result. The other rows evaluate
supplied grade vectors; this call does not attach their historical solver
bounds to the two-criterion loss. In particular, an income-only optimization
bound concerns income's objective, not the loss obtained by applying those
grades to both outcomes.

```{r a4-comparison-plot, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="All reports evaluated on pool A with weights .5/.5, withholding cost .20, and at most five grades. Supplied alternatives are evaluated actions, not new solves. The common report and expected-rank cuts coincide; withholding every pair has no defined error rate among ordered pairs."}
postrank_plot_compare(comparison)
```

Each separate report can also be evaluated under its own criterion. The
following table compares that loss with the corresponding criterion loss
in the common report:

```{r a4-single-criterion}
single <- alabama$reference$single_criterion
single_loss <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(single)), function(i) {
  criterion <- single$criterion[i]
  postrank_evaluate(alabama$reference$actions[[single$method[i]]],
    alabama$alternatives[[criterion]], weights = setNames(1, criterion),
    tau = settings$tau)$primary_risk
}, numeric(1))
common_loss <- profile$risk[match(single$criterion, profile$criterion)]
cost <- data.frame(Criterion = single$criterion,
  Common = common_loss, Separate = single_loss,
  Difference = common_loss - single_loss,
  Archived_gap = single$gap)
knitr::kable(cost, digits = 6, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Criterion", "Common loss", "Separate loss",
    "Extra loss for common grades", "Separate solver gap"))
```

The separate optimizations were recorded as optimal by postrank 0.9.0 with
HiGHS 1.12.0.3. Here their fixed grades are reevaluated and their archived
bounds retained, without repeating the full optimizations. The differences
quantify the loss incurred by requiring a common report instead of separate
outcome-specific reports. Their equal-weight average is
`r fmt(mean(cost$Difference), 6)`. This quantity is expressed in loss units;
it is neither a monetary cost nor a posterior credible interval. The
separate reports are also not an admissible replacement when a single
common grading is required.

## Numerical replication with fixed observations {#check-numerical-repetition-without-changing-the-observations}

Pool B is a separate numerical run using the same models and observations.
The source retained
`r num(alabama$reference$numerical_pools$source_draws_per_criterion[1])`
draws per criterion in A and
`r num(alabama$reference$numerical_pools$source_draws_per_criterion[2])` in B.
These are draw counts from the original runs; the package input contains
the resulting summaries. Pool B assesses numerical integration without
providing additional counties or independent observational replication.

We evaluate the fixed pool-A grades under both probability inputs:

```{r a4-pool-check}
ev_A <- postrank_evaluate(grades, alabama$input, settings = settings)
ev_B <- postrank_evaluate(grades, alabama$alternatives$pool_B,
  settings = settings)
pool_check <- data.frame(Pool = c("A", "B"),
  Fixed_report_loss = c(ev_A$primary_risk, ev_B$primary_risk),
  Ordered_pairs = c(ev_A$N, ev_B$N))
knitr::kable(pool_check, digits = 6, row.names = FALSE)
```

The loss changes by `r fmt(ev_B$primary_risk - ev_A$primary_risk, 6)`;
the number of ordered pairs stays fixed because the grade vector stays
fixed. The source also reselected a report using B and recorded
`r alabama$reference$relation_stability$changed_pairs[alabama$reference$relation_stability$comparison == "P_B_reselected"]`
changed pair relations relative to A. That is a descriptive numerical
stability result. Selecting and evaluating on B would not make B an
independent evaluation of the newly selected report.

Pool B did not meet the sensitive-pair Monte Carlo standard-error target
of .005 in
`r alabama$reference$numerical_pools$nonconstant_sensitive_failed_rows[2]`
directional criterion rows; its maximum was
`r fmt(alabama$reference$numerical_pools$maximum_nonconstant_sensitive_mcse[2], 6)`.
The archived Monte Carlo standard error for the fixed common report's
pool-B loss was
`r fmt(alabama$reference$metrics$B_Rtau_mcse[alabama$reference$metrics$method == "P"], 7)`,
which met the separate .001 fixed-risk target. Thus precision of the
aggregate loss can be satisfactory even when some sensitive pair
probabilities fail their precision criterion.

Those standard errors were calculated from the original chains and are
reported here from the source results. They are not recalculated from these
summaries. Constant-trace pair standard errors were unavailable; estimated
probabilities of zero or one are not proof of posterior certainty. Neither
the numerical repetition nor the optimizer's small gap validates the model
against new observations.

## Interpretation and scope {#use-the-result-and-retain-its-scope}

For these historical outcomes, the common grading withholds many county
comparisons, has different expected error rates across outcomes and agrees
with the expected-rank cut baseline. Separate reports address distinct
single-outcome losses. The choice between these formulations is substantive:
a lower risk under a different loss does not establish improvement for the
original decision problem.

Application to another setting requires specification of the population,
target directions, posterior model and intended use of the common grading.
The [posterior-input article](a5-your-posterior-results.html) describes input
preparation, [reading and exporting results](a6-reading-exporting-results.html)
documents the result tables, and [figures and sensitivity analysis](a7-figures-sensitivity.html)
examines changes to settings and figure presentation. A smaller introductory
example uses [one or several criteria](a1-getting-started.html).

The data source is Raj Chetty, John Friedman, Nathaniel Hendren, Maggie R.
Jones and Sonya R. Porter (2022), *Replication Data for: The Opportunity
Atlas: Mapping the Childhood Roots of Social Mobility*, Harvard Dataverse,
V1.0, [doi:10.7910/DVN/NKCQM1](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/NKCQM1).
Source: Opportunity Insights and the U.S. Census Bureau. The selected
[county CSV](https://opportunityinsights.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/county_outcomes_simple.csv)
and documented derivatives are used under
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
Changes include selecting Alabama, adding county identifiers and names,
converting display units, reversing the incarceration direction, fitting
separate posterior models, and preparing the probabilities and summaries
used here. The grades and interpretation are this example's analysis; no
endorsement by the original authors or agencies is implied. These are the
older historical county outcomes, distinct from a later policy-needs
analysis with different directions and targets.

[Posterior inputs](m3-posterior-inputs.html) specifies the probability information required by this loss. The [uncertainty article](m6-uncertainty-diagnostics.html) explains why a stable aggregate risk can coexist with less precise individual comparisons.
